headline: Smartphones and Ancient Skills Save Desert Lions in Namibia
meta_description: Community rangers in Namibia use real-time smartphone data and traditional tracking to protect lions and livestock, reducing conflict in the Kunene region.
summary_short: Desert lions are thriving again in Namibia, but their recovery creates conflict with farmers. Smart technology and local rangers are finding a balance.
body:
In north-west Namibia's Kunene region, community rangers are bridging ancient tracking wisdom with modern technology to protect both livestock and a recovering lion population. Operating across 11 conservancies over a 40,000 square-kilometre range, rangers like Benjamin Kordom now carry smartphones loaded with SMART software, allowing them to log observations in real time and coordinate rapid response teams. What began in 2018—when lions killed livestock on Kordom's farm—evolved into a systematic approach combining GPS collars on 44 lions, camera traps, and human patrols covering nearly 280,000 kilometres in just 18 months. The lions themselves tell the success story: Kunene's desert lion population rebounded from around 20 adults in 1997 to approximately 180 by 2015, a conservation triumph that created an unexpected problem.

Yet recovery brought tension. Since the mid-2010s, wild prey has fallen by around 72.5%, forcing lions to hunt livestock and venture near human settlements. The Lion Rangers programme addresses this directly. Kordom, now field coordinator overseeing more than 40 rangers and rapid response drivers, uses SMART data to anticipate conflicts and mobilise teams before tragedy strikes. Rangers walking 20 kilometres to warn remote farms of approaching lions, or gathering livestock to safety, have earned genuine community respect—a shift in attitudes that technology alone never could have achieved.

The work remains physically demanding and dangerous. Yet the system works because it honours both worlds: rangers' deep knowledge of the land and animal behaviour, combined with the transparency and coordination that real-time data enables. Every kilometre walked is timestamped and geo-tagged, creating accountability visible to government, donors, and conservancies. It's a model proving that coexistence between humans and apex predators isn't just possible—it can be measured, improved, and scaled.
quick_facts: Namibia's Kunene desert lions grew from 20 to 180 adults between 1997 and 2015
Benjamin Kordom oversees 40+ rangers across 40,000 square kilometres
Rangers logged nearly 280,000 kilometres of patrols in 18 months using SMART software
Community rangers use smartphones, GPS collars, and camera traps for real-time lion tracking
